hypothesis: Volatility scaling (#8) and trend exits (#2, #3, #7) both lost ground because each one sells in situations that usually end well. Trend exits whipsaw in calm, shallow dips. Volatility scaling sells high-volatility rebounds, which often carry high returns, as in 2020. The losses Moreira & Muir's effect protects against sit mostly in the overlap: high volatility while the market is already in a downtrend, where volatility persists and returns are poor. So this rule holds the index fully unless both signals agree. It cuts to min(1, 15%/realised vol) only when SPY is below its 200-day average and last month's volatility is above 15%, with the rest in short Treasuries. It should keep nearly all of buy-and-hold's upside, cut the deep bear-market falls, and trade far less than #7 or #8. It is proven wrong if it fails to beat SPY's CAGR in validation, or if its worst fall is no better than SPY's.
lesson: The overlap filter did what the drawdown half of the hypothesis predicted: it cut the worst fall in both periods, to -33.8% vs -55.2% in research and -25.0% vs -33.7% in validation. It failed the upside half by its own stated test, trailing buy-and-hold's validation CAGR by 3.5 points with turnover near 117%. That suggests the 2020-2023 V-shaped rebounds and choppy 2022 still met both conditions, so it de-risked and then re-entered late. Future ideas should stop adding variants of SPY timing filters, since every one so far gives up return in fast recoveries. They should look for return from a different source, such as cross-asset or diversification rules, and judge the whipsaw cost in validation-like regimes before claiming that drawdown protection comes nearly free.

hypothesis: Investors anchor on the 52-week high. Good news for a stock or sector trading near that high is absorbed slowly, so prices keep drifting up afterwards (George & Hwang 2004). Unlike 12-1 momentum, this signal mostly avoids momentum crashes, because names near their highs during a sell-off tend to be the ones holding up best. So the rule holds the 6 names closest to their 52-week closing high, equal-weighted at about 16.7% each and rebalanced monthly. The candidates are the 19 stocks plus the 9 sector ETFs, and the sector ETFs are included to dilute the survivorship bias. The ratio is averaged over the past month to cut rank noise and turnover. The idea is proven wrong if, after costs, it fails to beat both SPY and the equal-weight universe benchmark in validation. It is also proven wrong if its worst fall is deeper than buy-and-hold's in either period, or if turnover approaches the 300% limit.
lesson: The hypothesis failed by its own stated tests. Ranking 28 names by closeness to their 52-week high churned at over 500% a year even with the month-averaged ratio. It trailed the equal-weight universe by about 11 points a year in both periods and lost to SPY in validation, so the only real gain was a shallower worst fall, which the defensive sector ETFs that sit near their highs probably supplied rather than any slow-drift edge. Future ideas should build in turnover control from the start (for example, keep a holding until it drops well out of the top group, or rank only broad asset-class ETFs), and should not expect a stock-picking rule on this survivor-biased list to beat its own equal-weight benchmark.
caveats: Survivorship bias: the 19 single stocks are today's large-cap winners picked in 2026 (free data has no delisted stocks), so stock-picking results are biased upwards. The ETF part of the universe has traded continuously since 2006 and is not affected.

hypothesis: Stock momentum (trial #12_1 benchmark) has been the only rule that beat both SPY and the equal-weight universe. It failed this project's tests on two counts: it fell deeper than SPY in validation, and its turnover sat near the cap. Barroso & Santa-Clara (2015) show that momentum crashes are predictable from momentum's own recent volatility, because crash risk clusters when the winner basket becomes wild. So this rule holds the top 5 stocks by 12-1 momentum, but keeps a held name until it falls out of the top 8. The holdings path is replayed from the data each time, so the rule is stateless. Exposure is scaled to min(1, 25% / realised 6-month volatility of the held basket), with the rest in short Treasuries. 25% is roughly a concentrated mega-cap basket's normal volatility, so the rule is fully invested in normal times, and this level was not tuned. It is proven wrong if, after costs, it fails to beat the equal-weight universe CAGR in validation, if its worst fall is deeper than buy-and-hold's in either period, or if turnover is not clearly below the plain momentum benchmark's ~270%/yr.
lesson: The rank buffer clearly worked: turnover fell to about 170%/yr from plain momentum's ~270%. The volatility scaling did not deliver the promised crash protection. The validation drawdown of -33.6% only ties SPY's -33.7%, because a 6-month volatility window reacts too slowly to a sudden crash like early 2020. That makes the "passed" drawdown test a coin flip rather than evidence. Future ideas should treat the strong CAGR as inflated by survivorship bias until it is shown to beat the equal-weight universe, which is not reported here. They should also aim for drawdown control with a real margin, rather than shrinking or tweaking the volatility window to win back a 0.1-point edge.
caveats: Survivorship bias: the 19 single stocks are today's large-cap winners picked in 2026 (free data has no delisted stocks), so stock-picking results are biased upwards. The ETF part of the universe has traded continuously since 2006 and is not affected.
notes: stage B agent; screen = beat buy-and-hold and 5%/yr, fall no deeper, turnover <= 300%, stock pickers beat equal-weight, in both periods
